content: Influenza A viruses are categorized into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Among these, three hemagglutinin subtypes (H1, H2, H3) and two neuraminidase subtypes (N1, N2) have been identified as causing widespread human disease. Immunity to these antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and mitigates disease severity if infection occurs. However, infection with one subtype provides little to no protection against other subtypes. Additionally, antigenic drift within a subtype can lead to significant variation, rendering immunity from prior infection or vaccination ineffective against distantly related strains of the same subtype. Influenza B viruses exhibit greater antigenic stability compared to Influenza A viruses, but antigenic variation still occurs. This ongoing variation is why major epidemics of respiratory disease caused by new influenza variants continue to emerge. The antigenic properties of circulating strains guide the selection of virus strains included in the annual vaccine. Typical influenza illness presents with a sudden onset of fever, muscle aches, sore throat, and a dry cough. Unlike other common respiratory infections, influenza can cause severe fatigue lasting several days. More severe cases may involve primary influenza pneumonia or secondary bacterial pneumonia. During influenza epidemics, high attack rates of acute illness lead to increased visits to healthcare facilities and hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract complications. Elderly individuals and those with underlying health conditions are at higher risk for complications and are more likely to require hospitalization. During major epidemics, hospitalization rates for high-risk individuals can increase twoto fivefold, depending on the age group. Previously healthy children and young adults may also require hospitalization for influenza-related complications, though their relative increase in hospitalization rates is lower than that of high-risk groups. Influenza epidemics also result in increased mortality, not only from influenza and pneumonia but also from exacerbations of chronic diseases such as cardiopulmonary conditions. For example, during epidemics between 1957 and 1986, more than 40,000 excess deaths occurred in three separate epidemics, with 80%-90% of these deaths among individuals aged 65 years or older. As the population ages and chronic diseases become more prevalent, the burden of influenza is expected to rise unless control measures are implemented more effectively. Vaccination remains the most effective strategy for reducing the impact of influenza, particularly for high-risk individuals. Annual vaccination is necessary because immunity wanes over time, and the vaccine composition changes to match circulating strains. Vaccination is cost-effective, especially when targeted at high-risk individuals or those with increased exposure risk. Achieving high vaccination rates in closed populations can induce herd immunity, reducing the risk of outbreaks. Antiviral agents, such as amantadine, are effective against Influenza A but must be used throughout the risk period for maximum prophylactic benefit. However, chemoprophylaxis is not a substitute for vaccination. The inactivated influenza vaccine is made from purified, egg-grown viruses rendered noninfectious. It cannot cause influenza. Each year’s vaccine contains three virus strains (usually two type A and one type B) expected to circulate in the upcoming season. The vaccine rarely causes systemic or febrile reactions. Subvirion or purified surface-antigen preparations are recommended for children to minimize febrile reactions, while any preparation may be used for adults. Most vaccinated individuals develop protective antibody levels against strains similar to those in the vaccine. However, elderly individuals and those with chronic diseases may develop lower antibody levels and remain susceptible to upper respiratory tract infections. Nevertheless, the vaccine has been shown to prevent lower respiratory tract involvement and other complications, reducing hospitalization and mortality risks. Influenza vaccination is strongly recommended for individuals aged six months and older who are at increased risk of complications due to age or underlying medical conditions. Healthcare workers and household members in close contact with high-risk individuals should also be vaccinated. Pregnant women with medical conditions that increase their risk of complications should receive the vaccine, which is considered safe during pregnancy. Vaccination after the first trimester is a reasonable precaution to minimize theoretical risks, but delaying vaccination for high-risk pregnant women in their first trimester is undesirable. For individuals infected with HIV, vaccination is a prudent precaution, as influenza can cause prolonged symptoms and increased complications. Although antibody responses may be lower in those with advanced HIV-related illnesses, vaccination can still provide protection. Booster doses have not been shown to improve immune responses in these individuals. Foreign travelers, particularly those visiting the tropics or the Southern Hemisphere during influenza season, should review their vaccination history and consider vaccination if not previously immunized. High-risk travelers should receive the most current vaccine available. The inactivated influenza vaccine should not be given to individuals with a history of anaphylactic hypersensitivity to eggs. Those with acute febrile illnesses should delay vaccination until symptoms subside. The most common side effect is soreness at the injection site, lasting up to two days. Rarely, immediate allergic reactions, such as hives or anaphylaxis, may occur due to residual egg protein in the vaccine. Influenza vaccination can be administered simultaneously with other vaccines, such as pneumococcal or childhood vaccines, at different sites. However, it should not be given within three days of pertussis vaccination. Vaccination campaigns should begin in September, with November being the optimal time for organized efforts. High-risk individuals hospitalized during the influenza season should be vaccinated before discharge. Efforts to vaccinate healthcare workers and household members of high-risk individuals are essential to reduce transmission. Antiviral agents, such as amantadine, are effective against Influenza A but not Influenza B. When used prophylactically, amantadine is 70%-90% effective in preventing illness caused by type A influenza. For symptomatic treatment, it reduces the duration of fever and systemic symptoms if administered within 48 hours of symptom onset. However, the potential benefits of antiviral agents must be weighed against possible side effects.
